581: Law 12: Tripping, pushing or holding an opponent carelessly, recklessly or with excessive force is a direct free kick, or a penalty in the offender's own penalty area. Reckless = yellow, excessive force = red. An obvious goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO) is judged on four criteria: distance to goal, direction of play, likelihood of controlling the ball, and the number and position of defenders. A DOGSO foul in the penalty area while attempting to play the ball is reduced to a yellow, and a foul stopping a promising attack (SPA) to no card. This reduction does not apply to offences with no attempt to play the ball, such as holding, pushing or pulling. Simulation (diving as if fouled) is a yellow card and an indirect free kick to the opponents.
582: Law 12: It is an offence if a player deliberately touches the ball with the hand/arm, or if the hand/arm makes the body unnaturally bigger. An arm position not justified by the body's movement at that moment is unnatural; an arm above shoulder height is rarely justified. The upper limit of the arm is the bottom of the armpit. An arm supporting the body between the body and the ground when falling (not extended sideways or upwards) is not an offence. The ball rebounding from the player's own body is a mitigating factor. A player (other than a goalkeeper in their own penalty area) who denies an obvious goal with the hand is sent off.
583: Law 12: If an attacker scores immediately after the ball accidentally touches their hand/arm, the goal is disallowed. If after an accidental touch the ball goes to a team-mate who scores, that touch alone does not disallow the goal. Deliberately trying to score with the hand is a yellow card. The shoulder is not part of the arm; the upper limit of the arm is the bottom of the armpit.
584: Law 11: A player is in an offside position if, at the moment a team-mate plays the ball, they are in the opponents' half and any part of the head, body or feet is nearer to the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Arms and hands are not considered; being level is not offside. Being in an offside position is not an offence in itself: it becomes one if the player plays the ball, clearly obstructs an opponent's line of vision or clearly impacts an opponent's ability to play the ball. There is no offside directly from a throw-in, goal kick or corner kick. A deliberate play by an opponent resets offside; a reflex save or a deflection does not.
585: Law 12: A careless challenge is just a foul. A reckless challenge (disregard of the danger to an opponent) is a yellow card. Excessive force (endangering the opponent's safety, far beyond what is needed) is a red card — serious foul play. Studs showing, the height of contact, speed and intensity are the key indicators. Stopping a promising attack with a foul is a yellow card; if the referee plays advantage, that yellow is not needed. A second yellow card becomes a red.
586: Law 12: For DOGSO the four criteria are judged together: distance between the offence and the goal, general direction of play, likelihood of keeping control of the ball, and the location and number of defenders. Outside the penalty area DOGSO is always a red card. Lines belong to the areas they define: a foul on the penalty area line is a penalty, and the penalty-area DOGSO rules apply.
587: Law 12: In an aerial challenge, natural use of the arm for balance or jumping is not a foul. Using the arm as a lever or to push is reckless (yellow card). Swinging the elbow into an opponent's face/head is violent conduct (red card).
588: Law 12: Excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball is violent conduct: red card. A contact offence against an opponent while the ball is in play is a direct free kick, or a penalty if it happens in the offender's own penalty area. Offensive words or gestures are a red card; without contact, play restarts with an indirect free kick. For an offence while the ball is out of play, the disciplinary sanction is given and play restarts according to why it was stopped.
589: Law 12: Holding, pushing or impeding the goalkeeper with contact is a foul and the goal is disallowed. Normal shoulder contact between two players trying to play the ball is not a foul. A goalkeeper colliding with a team-mate is not an offence.
590: Law 10: A goal is scored when the whole of the ball passes over the goal line, between the goalposts and under the crossbar. Most of the ball crossing the line is not enough.
591: Law 12: If the goalkeeper handles the ball in their own penalty area after it has been deliberately kicked to them by a team-mate, an indirect free kick is awarded. Passes with the head, chest or knee, or uncontrolled deflections, are allowed. A player who uses a trick to get around the law (flicking the ball up to head it back) is cautioned, and the opponents take an indirect free kick. An indirect free kick inside the goal area is taken from the nearest point on the goal area line.
592: Law 12: An attacker who gains an advantage before a goal by pushing, holding or stepping on an opponent's foot commits a foul and the goal is disallowed. Normal shoulder-to-shoulder challenges and light balancing contact are not fouls.
593: Law 14: At the moment of the kick, the goalkeeper must have at least part of one foot touching, or in line with, the goal line. If the goalkeeper offends and the ball does not go in, the kick is retaken; if the ball goes wide (and the keeper did not affect the kicker), it is not retaken. The goalkeeper is warned for the first offence and cautioned for further offences. If the kicker feints after completing the run-up: indirect free kick and yellow card. Attacker encroaches: retake if scored, otherwise indirect free kick. Defender encroaches: goal stands if scored, otherwise retake.
